The least complex design is usually a long-running worker process, not a web request stretched until a timeout gives up.
For an education platform, a useful message might say that tenant school-42 has 18,240 expired upload records to remove. The web application records that work and returns. A worker reads it later, processes a bounded batch, and leaves a precise trail of what happened. Recovery is the design target: when the worker disappears between deleting records and acknowledging the message, the next delivery must be safe.
That is the whole contract.

articles.description:
For a healthtech renewal reminder, this Node.js setup creates a message queue and publishes a background task that must wait until a business deadline, survive a worker restart, and remain explainable when an operator has to recover it. My default design is a durable job record plus a queue message carrying an idempotency key. The worker claims the message, checks the deadline again, sends once, and acknowledges only after the side effect succeeds.
That last check matters. A queue delay is an implementation detail. The deadline is the business rule.

articles.description:
You build a Slack agent that pulls GitHub issues, creates Jira tickets, and sends Stripe invoices. Ten people use it. Each person signs in with their own account. The agent uses a single service credential.
Who is allowed to see which issues? Who can create invoices? When the agent makes 50 API calls in one user request, whose permissions apply?
This is the multi-user agent access control problem. OAuth was designed for one user, one session, one token. Agents break that model because the agent is the shared actor, but the authorization boundary must still enforce per-user permissions.
Most internal agents start with a service account. You generate one GitHub token, one Slack bot token, one Stripe key. You paste them into .env and ship.

articles.author: Damin Mutti
articles.description:
Wells Fargo statements print an ending daily balance only on the last transaction of each day, leaving the column blank on other rows. That half-empty column is a free test for a parser: group rows by date, add each day's amounts to a running total, and compare with the printed balance.
A mismatch tells you which day lost or mangled a row, not just that the month is off.
I'm on the ZeraBooks team, where we convert a lot of these. The usual advice is "check that the month ties to the ending balance," which is right but coarse: a month that's off by 425.00 could be off anywhere in 30 days. The daily balance narrows it to one day, and it's sitting in the statement already.
A Wells Fargo business checking statement typically prints one transaction table with columns for date, check number, des…
articles.title: Wells Fargo statements: using the half-empty 'Ending daily balance' column as a free parser test

Most Large Language Model (LLM) applications currently deployed in production are not autonomous; they are fragile dependencies wrapped in HTTP calls that break the moment the model outputs an unexpected JSON key or fails to follow a multi-step instruction set. Engineers are spending the majority of their sprint capacity "babysitting" these models—manually injecting context, retrying failed generations, and hard-coding exception handlers for every possible hallucination. The result is brittle systems that require constant human supervision, effectively turning an AI-powered feature into a high-maintenance manual workflow.
